examples.before:
a:
  b: 1
  c: 2  # keep
e: {}
l: []
name: demo

results.1: exit 0, no output; file becomes `a: 5` and the `# keep` comment is lost
results.2: four arms: exit 0, `a: 5`, comment lost; one arm: exit 0, `a: 5  # keep` (comment kept)

examples.input: `config set e 7` then `config set a "{x: 1}"` then `config get a.x`

results.1: file has `e: 7` and `a:` / `  x: 1`; `get a.x` prints `1`
results.2: all five arms: same file and `get a.x` prints `1`; the comment-keeping arm writes `a:    # keep` / `  x: 1`

results.1: imports a.b, a.c, name; then `set a 5`, `remove a.b`, `remove a.c` (parent set logged before the child removes); `set e 7`; then `set a.x 1` followed by `remove a` (old 5)
results.2: four arms: same order as route 1; one arm: `remove a.b`, `remove a.c` before `set a 5`, and `remove a` before `set a.x 1`

context.in_practice: Every arm on both routes gave the same exit codes, files and `get` output, apart from one route-2 arm that kept the comment. Route 1 and four of the five route-2 arms log a parent's new value before removing its old children, so replaying those logs in order produces removes for paths that are already gone. Route 1 is built to ignore those removes, but no replay was actually run here, so how each route handles those removes was not observed. The route-2 arm that logs removes first never produces such events.
context.stakes: When a whole section is replaced by a single value (or the reverse), the history log decides what a later replay rebuilds. Here that means the events written for `a` and its children `a.b` and `a.c`. If removes of paths that no longer exist are not handled, replaying old history could fail or rebuild the wrong config.
context.tradeoff: Route 1 has to ignore removes of missing paths, which could also hide a remove that really is wrong. Route 2 never considered this case, so whether replay fails or silently skips them was not tested, and its arms produced two different log orders.

plan_why: Replaces a mapping and an empty mapping with scalars and back, which can record remove events for paths that were never leaves. Later commands then rebuild the configuration from those events: route 1 skips the unknown paths, while an implementation without that guard may crash (non-zero exit or traceback) or report wrong values or history.
